title: What a rise in ECB borrowing would tell us about banks
summary: Isabel Schnabel offers a way to distinguish two very different uses of an ECB balance sheet. An overnight rate expresses the Governing Council’s desired monetary stance. Supplying a solvent bank with reserves against collateral helps the payment and funding system operate at that stance. As the ECB’s old bond portfolios mature, refinancing volumes can rise even if the Council leaves rates unchanged. At the Money Markets Conference, Schnabel described how the pattern of that borrowing could guide the composition of the balance sheet. These were her reflections as an Executive Board member, including her own preferred sequence for future operations.

Her starting point is a forecasting failure. Before the pandemic the ECB repeatedly projected more inflation than subsequently materialised. After the pandemic the errors changed sign. The weighted distribution of prices in slide 3 shows why an average alone gave an incomplete signal: more goods and services were registering increases above 2%. Firms were repricing more often. The decomposition in slide 5 compares contributions to the GDP deflator through 1975 and through mid-2023. Rising profits per unit of output made a substantial contribution in the recent episode, while rising labour costs per unit of output had dominated the earlier one. A wage-only model would have missed an important source of domestic inflation.

Schnabel’s criticism of pandemic-era forward guidance follows from that experience. A commitment built for persistent inflation shortfalls became costly once policymakers began repeatedly underestimating price pressure. The time needed to reverse an instrument matters as much as the public language used to announce it. A policy rate can change at a meeting. The stock of bonds accumulated through purchases continues to affect the compensation investors demand to hold duration after new purchases end. Her case for retaining asset purchases is strongest when a market has abruptly lost liquidity or when rates have reached their effective lower bound. The Transmission Protection Instrument illustrates how to address disorderly conditions in a particular market while retaining freedom over the policy rate.

The immediate inflation question is how far an energy shock will travel. Services inflation was already above 3% before the Middle East conflict. Wages negotiated at different dates continued to catch up with earlier price increases. Household expectations at medium and longer horizons had moved away from the target in the survey she presented. She treats those observations as reasons to investigate persistence. They do not establish that wages have accelerated in response to the newest shock. Climate damage, energy disruption, domestic investment and fiscal demand can overlap. Their joint effect on expected inflation matters for the rate decision even when the source of the first price increase lies outside the country.

The same risk of amplification arises in sovereign debt markets. Schnabel puts the increase in euro-area public debt since the early 2000s at nearly 20 percentage points of GDP, with wide differences across countries. Private investors absorb more government debt as central banks shrink portfolios. A hedge fund financing bonds in the repo market sees higher short-term rates in its funding costs quickly. A collateral markdown or a margin call can then force it to sell. A treasury that issues for shorter periods also refinances more quickly. This combination can sharpen transmission in ordinary conditions and disrupt it in volatile markets, especially where banks depend on non-bank intermediaries for funding. Her proposed remedies span tougher non-bank oversight, sound bank capital, national fiscal credibility and a stronger capacity for European firms to grow.

The operational proposal turns those arguments into an observable sequence. Banks can obtain their requested liquidity weekly at a fixed rate against eligible collateral. Recent operations spanning a month-end or year-end attracted demand from a broad set of banks. A single reporting-date spike says little about lasting reserve demand. If volumes stayed elevated outside those dates, longer-term structural loans could spare banks repeated weekly refinancing. Schnabel would introduce those loans while the legacy portfolios still supply substantial reserves and build a structural securities portfolio later. Standard refinancing would continue to provide the last unit of reserves banks want. There is a practical distinction for a bond desk here: rising use of collateralised credit, passive runoff of older bond purchases and the eventual purchase of securities for operating purposes can all occur without a new easing decision.

questions.question: Does refinancing demand persist beyond reporting dates?
questions.detail: Track the distribution of weekly allotments, the number of counterparties where published, and secured and unsecured rates around month- and year-ends. Compare borrowing before and after the turn against the path of reserve runoff. Repeated take-up on ordinary weeks would be stronger evidence of structural reserve demand than one large allotment and would make the case for term operations more relevant.

questions.question: Is the latest energy shock passing through prices more quickly than wages?
questions.detail: Recreate slide 3’s weighted inflation distribution and track how often firms change prices before and after the energy increase. Compare the sequence with unit profits, negotiated wages and the same household survey horizons used in slide 8. Faster price revisions followed by stable wages would support a margins or input-cost channel before it supported a wage-price feedback interpretation.

questions.question: Where would tighter repo funding start to affect sovereign transmission?
questions.detail: Compare sovereign collateral haircuts, repo spreads, bond-market depth and the maturity of new issuance across issuers. A jump in funding costs accompanied by widening bid–ask spreads would give the deleveraging channel more weight. Changes in yields alone also capture inflation expectations and a common revision to the expected path of short rates.
